content: 1. Engaging in any amount of physical activity is better than remaining inactive. 2. Older adults who are not meeting the recommended levels of physical activity can still experience health benefits by engaging in some physical activity. 3. It is advisable for older adults to begin with small amounts of physical activity and gradually increase the frequency, intensity, and duration over time. 4. Higher levels of sedentary behavior in older adults are associated with adverse health outcomes, including increased risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, cancer mortality, and the incidence of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and type-2 diabetes. 5. Older adults should aim to limit the amount of time spent being sedentary. 6. Replacing sedentary time with physical activity of any intensity, including light-intensity activity, provides health benefits. 7. To mitigate the harmful effects of prolonged sedentary behavior, older adults should strive to exceed the recommended levels of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity. 8. Physical activity in older adults improves health outcomes such as reduced all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, incident hypertension, site-specific cancers, type-2 diabetes, mental health (e.g., reduced symptoms of anxiety and depression), cognitive health, and sleep quality. It may also improve measures of adiposity. 9. Regular physical activity in older adults helps prevent falls, fall-related injuries, and declines in bone health and functional ability. 10. Older adults may increase their moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity to more than 300 minutes per week, or engage in more than 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity, or perform an equivalent combination of moderateand vigorous-intensity activity throughout the week for additional health benefits. 11. Older adults should also engage in muscle-strengthening activities of moderate or greater intensity that involve all major muscle groups on two or more days per week, as these activities provide additional health benefits. 12. As part of their weekly physical activity, older adults should perform varied, multicomponent physical activities that emphasize functional balance and strength training at moderate or greater intensity on three or more days per week to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. 13. All older adults should undertake regular physical activity, with a strong recommendation supported by moderate-certainty evidence. 14. Older adults should aim for at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity, or at least 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity, or an equivalent combination of moderateand vigorous-intensity activity throughout the week for substantial health benefits. 15. Pregnant and postpartum women should engage in regular physical activity throughout pregnancy and the postpartum period, provided there are no contraindications. 16. Physical activity during pregnancy and postpartum offers maternal and fetal health benefits, including reduced risk of pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension, gestational diabetes, excessive gestational weight gain, delivery complications, postpartum depression, and fewer newborn complications. It does not adversely affect birth weight or increase the risk of stillbirth. 17. Pregnant women who were habitually engaged in vigorous-intensity aerobic activity or were physically active before pregnancy can continue these activities during pregnancy and postpartum. 18. Pregnant and postpartum women should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity throughout the week for substantial health benefits. 19. Incorporating a variety of aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities, along with gentle stretching, may be beneficial for pregnant and postpartum women. 20. Pregnant and postpartum women should avoid physical activity in excessive heat, especially with high humidity, and should stay hydrated by drinking water before, during, and after physical activity. 21. Pregnant women should avoid activities involving physical contact, a high risk of falling, or those that may limit oxygenation (e.g., high-altitude activities if not accustomed to such environments). 22. After the first trimester, pregnant women should avoid activities performed in the supine position. 23. Pregnant women considering athletic competition or exercising significantly above the recommended guidelines should seek supervision from a specialist healthcare provider. 24. Pregnant women should be informed by their healthcare provider about danger signs that indicate when to stop or limit physical activity and consult a qualified healthcare provider immediately if these occur. 25. Adults and older adults with chronic conditions should limit the amount of time spent being sedentary. 26. Replacing sedentary time with physical activity of any intensity, including light-intensity activity, provides health benefits. 27. Adults and older adults with chronic conditions should aim to exceed the recommended levels of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity to reduce the detrimental effects of prolonged sedentary behavior. 28. Adults and older adults with chronic conditions, such as cancer survivors, or those living with hypertension, type-2 diabetes, or HIV, should engage in regular physical activity. 29. Adults and older adults with chronic conditions should aim for at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity, or at least 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity, or an equivalent combination of moderateand vigorous-intensity activity throughout the week for substantial health benefits. 30. When not contraindicated, adults and older adults with chronic conditions may increase their moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity to more than 300 minutes per week, or engage in more than 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity, or perform an equivalent combination of moderateand vigorous-intensity activity throughout the week for additional health benefits. 31. As part of their weekly physical activity, adults and older adults with chronic conditions should perform varied, multicomponent physical activities that emphasize functional balance and strength training at moderate or greater intensity on three or more days per week to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. 32. Adults and older adults with chronic conditions should also engage in muscle-strengthening activities of moderate or greater intensity that involve all major muscle groups on two or more days per week, as these activities provide additional health benefits.
